slides.title: Accuracy and premature responding are distinct
body: **Attention** selects information relevant to an ongoing goal; **response inhibition** withholds an action until it is appropriate. Bari and colleagues trained mice to wait 7 s for a light that appeared for 0.5 s in one of two apertures. A nose poke into the illuminated aperture earned food.

Correct-response proportion indexed target selection, whereas **premature responses**, nose pokes before target onset, indexed failure to wait. Incorrect choices and premature actions were therefore distinct outcomes within the same preparation. Light-driven neural activation altered both measures without changing response speed.

A mouse can select the wrong location after waiting correctly, or respond too early before any target exists. The task separates these errors operationally; neither alone constitutes a clinical diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or **ADHD**. Sensory, motivational and motor controls remain necessary when interpreting altered performance.

slides.title: Impulsive action differs from impulsive choice
body: **Impulsive action** refers to inadequate restraint of a response; **impulsive choice** refers to preference for an immediate outcome over a more valuable delayed outcome. Kim and colleagues examined action restraint in spontaneously hypertensive rats, or **SHR**, using drinking that incurred an aversive consequence.

After training, drinking for at least 5 s triggered a 0.5-s, 2-mA foot shock. SHR entered the water area and completed punished drinking more often than Wistar-Kyoto, or **WKY**, controls. The preparation measures persistence despite punishment rather than choosing between different reward delays.

Premature nose pokes and punished drinking are related measures of action control, but their sensory cues, reinforcement and motivational demands differ. A **phenotype** is an observable characteristic under specified conditions. An animal phenotype resembling one ADHD-associated behavior does not reproduce the complete human disorder or identify its cause.

slides.title: A sensory rule determines which stimulus guides choice
body: **Selective attention** prioritizes one information source while competing information is present. Wimmer and colleagues trained mice to choose a reward location from conflicting visual and auditory signals. A preceding sound instructed the animal which sensory modality, vision or hearing, should govern its response.

One cue used noise low-pass filtered at 10 kHz; another used noise high-pass filtered at 11 kHz. Their assignments were counterbalanced across animals. Visual trials required locating a light, whereas auditory trials required distinguishing an upward from a downward frequency sweep.

Successful performance required the instructed rule rather than following whichever stimulus was most salient. Counterbalancing reduced the possibility that one cue intrinsically favored one modality. Because visual detection and auditory discrimination differ computationally, balanced accuracy does not establish identical processing demands or identical sensory pathways.

slides.title: Selection costs persist when a distractor is omitted
body: Wimmer and colleagues measured a **detection threshold**, the stimulus strength associated with a specified level of visual performance. They varied light intensity while comparing visual-only trials with trials requiring a cue-dependent switch between vision and audition. Brief visual targets lasted 0.1 s during these measurements.

Visual detection required greater stimulus intensity under cross-modal conditions. Removing the conflicting auditory target did not restore the visual-only detection function. Conversely, learning over a session that auditory stimuli were unrewarded did not produce the same threshold change as trial-by-trial modality selection.

The cost therefore depends on the instructed task configuration, rather than merely acoustic interference from a simultaneous distractor. Expectation and sensory selection can modify measured visual sensitivity. This behavioral comparison does not by itself locate the circuit that changes sensitivity or distinguish every possible contribution of uncertainty and task switching.

slides.title: Flies balance fixation against wide-field motion
body: Kirszenblat and colleagues measured visual selection in freely walking _Drosophila melanogaster_. **Fixation** was orientation toward a target stripe; an **optomotor response** was turning with wide-field motion. Wing-clipped flies walked on a platform inside an illuminated arena, allowing both behaviors to be measured in the same animal.

Targets flickered at 7 Hz, while a background grating moved at 54 degrees per second with a temporal frequency of 3 Hz. **Target deviation**, the angle between walking direction and the target, increased as distractor contrast increased. Angular turning velocity separately measured motion-following behavior.

Competition altered orientation even though flies retained responses to isolated targets and motion. These measurements support attention-like selection in insects without assuming that their neural architecture duplicates mammalian frontal circuits. Target deviation measures behavior, not conscious experience, clinical inattention or a directly recorded attention neuron.

slides.title: Locus-coeruleus neurons supply cortical norepinephrine
body: The **locus coeruleus**, or LC, is a brainstem nucleus whose neurons release **norepinephrine**, or NE, a chemical transmitter that modulates target-cell activity. NE and **dopamine**, or DA, belong to the catecholamine transmitter family. Bari and colleagues targeted LC neurons genetically and verified their identity in labeled tissue.

A **transporter** moves transmitter across a cell membrane. Expression of the norepinephrine transporter, or **NET**, helped identify the targeted neurons. Fluorescent markers localized light-sensitive proteins in LC cells and noradrenergic axon terminals in frontal cortex; source micrographs retain 100-µm and 50-µm reference scales.

The anatomical evidence links a transmitter-defined population to cortical projections. An **axon terminal** is the release-bearing ending of a neuronal process. Labeling establishes location and molecular identity, but it does not alone establish when release occurs, which receptor responds or whether a projection changes behavior.

slides.title: Light-driven LC activity increases cortical NE release
body: **Optogenetics** controls genetically targeted cells with light-sensitive proteins. Bari and colleagues expressed **channelrhodopsin-2**, or ChR2, a light-activated ion channel, in noradrenergic neurons. Channel opening permitted depolarization, a shift of membrane voltage toward excitation, and increased LC firing during blue-light stimulation.

The investigators paired 7-s stimulation with 10-ms light pulses at different frequencies. At 20 Hz and 1.5 mW, stimulation produced elevated LC output and a robust prefrontal NE signal. A fluorescent NE sensor in medial prefrontal cortex reported transmitter-related changes during stimulation.

An imposed pulse frequency is not automatically the neuronal firing rate: this protocol elevated sustained LC firing to approximately 5 Hz. Sensor fluorescence provides an extracellular transmitter readout rather than a direct count of released molecules. Together, electrical recording and transmitter photometry validate the manipulation beyond protein expression alone.

slides.title: LC activation improves accuracy and waiting
body: During the two-choice task, Bari and colleagues activated LC neurons over the 7-s delay preceding the target. ChR2-expressing mice made more correct choices and fewer premature responses with the laser on. Littermate controls lacking the active protein received comparable illumination.

The brief 0.5-s target challenged accurate detection and selection. Activation did not shorten response times, and the stimulation protocol did not increase open-field locomotor distance. Food-related controls also argued against a simple increase in reward motivation as the explanation for improved task performance.

**Causal perturbation** tests whether deliberately changing neural activity changes an outcome. These results support an influence of LC activity on selection and restraint during preparation. They do not establish that every frequency, duration or behavioral state of LC activation is beneficial, or identify one cortical receptor responsible for both effects.

slides.title: LC suppression impairs accuracy and waiting
body: Bari and colleagues expressed **archaerhodopsin**, or Arch, a light-driven proton pump, in noradrenergic neurons. Its activation suppressed LC electrical activity. Applying continuous illumination during the delay provided a complementary manipulation to the ChR2 activation experiment.

In the task with a 7-s waiting period and a 0.5-s target, LC suppression reduced correct responses and increased premature nose pokes. Response times did not change. Animals lacking Arch served as illumination controls, while electrical recordings verified that the pump suppressed the targeted neurons.

Opposite behavioral effects of activation and suppression strengthen the causal connection between LC output and attentional control under these conditions. They do not imply that attention is a single variable determined by overall LC activity. The same nucleus has multiple projections, and suppressing its output can affect more than one downstream circuit.

slides.title: Irrelevant spatial cues alter response timing
body: A **valid cue** appears on the future target side; an **invalid cue** appears on the opposite side. Bari and colleagues also used neutral and absent cues. The cue lasted 0.5 s and preceded a 3-s target, but its position did not predict where reward-relevant information would appear.

Control mice responded more slowly following invalid than neutral cues. The **validity effect** compared response timing after invalid and valid cues. LC activation reduced this timing difference, whereas LC suppression increased it. The uninformative cues could therefore bias orientation even when following them was not a reliable strategy.

A smaller cue effect is consistent with stronger goal-directed selection of the target. Faster responding alone would not establish improved attention; changes must be interpreted relative to cue condition and accuracy. This preparation tests resistance to spatial distraction rather than all forms of vigilance, learning or impulsive choice.

slides.title: Calcium photometry samples ongoing LC activity
body: **Intracellular calcium** is a signaling ion whose concentration often changes with neuronal activity. Bari and colleagues expressed **GCaMP6f**, a calcium-sensitive fluorescent protein, in NET-positive LC neurons. Fiber photometry recorded the population signal while mice performed the cue-dependent two-choice task.

Activity was aligned to target onset, separating delay-period signals from cue- and target-evoked responses. Sensory-evoked activity was measured over 0.5-s windows. A wavelength that did not depend on calcium provided a comparison channel for separating activity-related fluorescence from some optical artifacts.

A calcium transient is a time-varying fluorescence response, rather than a direct measurement of every action potential. Population photometry averages signals from multiple cells and cannot establish whether individual projection-defined neurons respond identically. Its temporal relationship to behavior complements, but does not replace, electrical recording and causal manipulation.

slides.title: Prefrontal activity is required during sensory preparation
body: The **prelimbic cortex** is a medial prefrontal region in mice. Wimmer and colleagues disrupted its activity by stimulating local **GABAergic neurons**, cells that release the inhibitory transmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid, or GABA. Activation of these inhibitory cells reduced activity in the surrounding excitatory network.

Blue-light pulses at 50 Hz were delivered during either anticipation or target presentation. Prefrontal disruption impaired cross-modal performance when applied during anticipation. Comparable manipulation did not alter visual-only performance, even when the visual task was difficult; histology and light-spread measurements verified the targeted tissue.

The result supports a prefrontal requirement for preparing a cue-dependent sensory selection. It does not imply that all difficult visual decisions require the same frontal circuit. Timing-specific perturbations distinguish a preparatory contribution from direct sensory processing after the stimulus appears.

slides.title: Visual cortex contributes when the stimulus is present
body: The **primary visual cortex**, or V1, is a cortical region that processes visual input. Wimmer and colleagues used light-driven local inhibition to compare its contribution during anticipation with its contribution during presentation of the visual target. The original anatomical targeting accompanies the perturbation results.

Disruption during target presentation impaired visual performance, whereas anticipatory disruption did not produce the prefrontal pattern. In a visual-only task, visual-cortex perturbation increased the detection threshold. The same general 50-Hz stimulation approach therefore produced different effects depending on location and timing.

These results support a sensory-processing role for V1 under the tested conditions. They do not exclude cortical attentional modulation in other tasks or species. slides.title: Reticular neurons inhibit a visual thalamic relay
body: The **thalamus** contains nuclei linking sensory input with cortical processing. The **lateral geniculate nucleus**, or LGN, is a visual relay. The **thalamic reticular nucleus**, or TRN, is a surrounding population of inhibitory neurons; its visual sector, **visTRN**, projects to the LGN.

Wimmer and colleagues combined genetic identity with projection tracing to label GABAergic neurons connected to the LGN. **Retrograde labeling** identifies cells by transport from a projection target back toward their cell bodies. Original histology localized reticular and geniculate tissue with 100-µm reference scales.

This preparation identifies a candidate inhibitory route for regulating visual transmission. It does not make the TRN a passive barrier or establish that every reticular cell performs the same computation. Projection identity must be combined with activity during selection and perturbation of those identified neurons.

slides.title: Reticular activity depends on the selected modality
body: Wimmer and colleagues recorded spikes from projection-defined visTRN neurons while mice anticipated conflicting auditory and visual targets. Optogenetic identification linked the recorded cells to the previously labeled inhibitory population rather than relying only on electrode position. Firing rates were expressed in spikes per second, or hertz.

VisTRN activity decreased when the animal prepared to select vision and increased when it prepared to select audition. Disrupting prefrontal activity diminished this modality-dependent difference. The effect was not simply reproduced by naturally occurring errors, supporting a specific relationship to the preparatory frontal manipulation.

The pattern is consistent with reduced inhibition of the visual relay when vision is relevant and increased inhibition when it is distracting. Functional dependence on prefrontal activity does not by itself establish one direct monosynaptic connection. A **monosynaptic connection** is a link across a single synapse, which requires additional circuit evidence.

slides.title: Reticular perturbations bias sensory selection
body: Wimmer and colleagues activated or inhibited the LGN-projecting reticular population during the divided-attention task. ChR2 activation increased activity, whereas **halorhodopsin**, a light-driven chloride pump, suppressed it. Projection tracing and histology constrained the manipulated neurons to the visual inhibitory subnetwork.

Activation impaired visual-selection trials, consistent with excessive inhibition of the visual relay. Suppression preferentially impaired auditory-selection trials, when visual information needed to be disregarded. Perturbations were compared during anticipation and target presentation rather than treating the complete trial as one undifferentiated time period.

The opposing effects support a causal role for regulated reticular inhibition in selecting the relevant modality. Simply increasing visual transmission is not beneficial when vision is the distractor. These results establish task-dependent behavioral consequences, while the precise downstream electrical and chemical changes require recordings from the relay itself.

slides.title: Geniculate gain rises when vision is selected
body: **Sensory gain** describes the strength of a neural response to input under a particular processing state. Wimmer and colleagues recorded LGN neurons during the cross-modal task. Head-mounted lights reduced variability in retinal stimulation associated with changes in the animal’s position relative to wall-mounted targets.

LGN neurons had higher baseline and visually evoked firing when vision was selected than when audition was selected. The **visual evoked potential**, a stimulus-linked extracellular electrical signal, also increased. Recorded responses were aligned to light onset, with neuronal rates measured in hertz and evoked potentials in microvolts.

The results locate attention-dependent modulation within the visual thalamus, rather than only in a behavioral score. They do not identify which input changes the gain. Increased excitation and reduced inhibition can both elevate firing, so the inhibitory mechanism requires an additional physiological measurement and intervention.

slides.title: Chloride measurements connect selection to inhibition
body: The **GABA-A receptor** is a transmitter-gated ion channel that permits chloride movement. Wimmer and colleagues expressed **SuperClomeleon**, a chloride-sensitive fluorescent indicator, in LGN neurons. Its paired fluorescent proteins report **fluorescence resonance energy transfer**, or FRET, an energy-transfer signal that changes with intracellular chloride.

Excitation at 430 nm allowed a ratio of the two emission signals to be measured. Visual stimulation produced a larger chloride-related response when audition was selected. Reticular inactivation eliminated that modality-dependent difference; drug and fluorescent-protein controls supported the signal’s relationship to GABA-mediated inhibition.

The combined measurements support regulated inhibitory input as a mechanism of visual gain control. Bulk photometry does not isolate every synapse or supply a complete conductance measurement. A chloride-sensitive signal must be interpreted with its calibration and controls, rather than equating any fluorescence change with neuronal inhibition.

slides.title: NET contributes to frontal dopamine clearance
body: **Reuptake** removes extracellular transmitter by transporting it into cells. The **dopamine transporter**, or DAT, and NET differ in their regional abundance and substrate selectivity. Morón and colleagues used mouse transporter deletions to test whether NET contributes to dopamine uptake in frontal cortex.

They measured radiolabeled dopamine accumulation in **synaptosomes**, isolated resealed nerve-terminal preparations. Incubation at 37°C was compared with a 4°C background control. Frontal dopamine uptake was retained after DAT deletion but reduced after NET deletion; the wild-type frontal rate was 0.45 pmol per minute per milligram of protein.

The result establishes a transporter contribution to uptake in this isolated preparation. It does not directly measure dopamine release, ongoing behavior or receptor stimulation in an intact animal. A transporter’s name identifies its usual association, rather than guaranteeing that it transports only the corresponding transmitter.

body: Morón and colleagues compared frontal cortex with the **caudate**, part of the dorsal striatum, and the **nucleus accumbens**, a ventral striatal region. slides.title: Medication effects vary across dose and individual
body: Gamo and colleagues tested **methylphenidate**, which inhibits catecholamine uptake, and **atomoxetine**, a relatively selective NET inhibitor, on macaque spatial working memory. Food was hidden in a well, and the animal selected its remembered location after an opaque screen interrupted visibility. Vehicle treatments controlled for administration without active drug.

Oral methylphenidate doses ranged from 0.1 to 2.0 mg/kg; atomoxetine ranged from 0.001 to 5.0 mg/kg. Individual dose-response curves generally formed an **inverted U**: intermediate exposure improved performance, whereas lower or higher exposure did not consistently help and could impair it.

body: A **knockout** removes functional expression of a gene. slides.title: Hyperactivity and cognitive deficits can coexist
body: Leo and colleagues measured locomotion and cognition in DAT-knockout rats rather than treating one assay as the complete phenotype. Movement was elevated in both home-cage recordings and novel test chambers. Twenty-four-hour recordings also distinguished light- and dark-period activity.

Knockout animals displayed lower spontaneous alternation and impaired **prepulse inhibition**, reduced suppression of a startle response when a weaker sound precedes the startling stimulus. Methylphenidate at 1.5–5 mg/kg reduced knockout hyperlocomotion, whereas it increased locomotion in transporter-intact animals.

A medication-related reduction in movement is not itself proof of restored attention or a diagnosis of ADHD. The same genetic manipulation changes transmitter clearance, behavior and developmental physiology. Spontaneous alternation and sensorimotor gating identify additional impairments, but neither directly establishes a premature-response deficit in the two-choice attention task.

slides.title: Lphn3 loss changes prefrontal dopamine decay
body: **Latrophilin-3**, encoded by _Lphn3_, is an adhesion G-protein-coupled receptor associated with synapse formation. Sable and colleagues compared knockout rats with wild-type littermates using **fixed-potential amperometry**, an electrochemical method that records oxidation current at a constant electrode potential. Rats were anesthetized during these measurements.

The medial forebrain bundle was stimulated at 50 Hz; prefrontal measurements used 50 pulses of 0.5-ms duration. Medial-prefrontal dopamine peak amplitude did not differ by genotype, but the **half-life**, the time for the evoked increase to fall by half, was longer in knockout rats.

The result supports slower prefrontal signal decay without a detected difference in the measured release peak. Half-life is a clearance-related readout, not direct proof of a DAT-specific mechanism in low-DAT cortex. NET-mediated uptake and other removal processes complicate a transporter-specific interpretation; ongoing task-related attention was not measured during anesthesia.

slides.title: SHR dopamine differences are region-specific
body: Sable and colleagues used the same stimulation-and-amperometry strategy to compare SHR with WKY controls. **Phasic signaling** is a transient change associated with brief neuronal activity, distinct from a sustained background concentration. Recordings sampled medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens core separately.

SHR had lower stimulation-evoked dopamine release in accumbens core, but no detected strain difference in prefrontal peak amplitude or half-life. Accumbens half-life also did not differ. Accumbens stimulation used 20 pulses at 50 Hz, whereas prefrontal stimulation used 50 pulses at the same frequency.

The result argues against a uniform dopamine deficit across the sampled regions. A regional release ratio is not a direct measurement of communication or electrical coherence between the regions. Different stimulation protocols and anatomical sampling must be retained when comparing the absolute sizes of cortical and accumbens signals.

slides.title: Rat models respond differently to uptake inhibition
body: Sable and colleagues administered **nomifensine**, a catecholamine uptake inhibitor used here to test dopamine-clearance-related responses. A 10-mg/kg intraperitoneal dose was followed by accumbens-core measurements, with the 20-min response compared against each animal’s predrug baseline. **Intraperitoneal** administration delivers a substance into the abdominal cavity.

Nomifensine increased the evoked dopamine peak proportionally more in Lphn3-knockout than wild-type rats. The corresponding percent change did not differ between SHR and WKY controls. The drug-related half-life change did not differ by genotype or strain, and the measured autoreceptor responses also lacked a group difference.

An **autoreceptor** detects a neuron’s own transmitter and can regulate subsequent release. These results distinguish model-specific responses to the same intervention, rather than identifying one universal ADHD dopamine mechanism. Percent-of-baseline amplification does not establish identical absolute concentrations, clinical treatment efficacy or attention improvement.

slides.title: Sleep loss selectively weakens competition performance
body: Kirszenblat and colleagues sleep-deprived flies for 24 h using repeated mechanical stimulation. Sleep was operationally scored as at least 5 min of immobility. Deprived animals exhibited subsequent **sleep rebound**, increased sleep following its loss, and were tested on target fixation competing with visual motion.

Sleep loss increased target deviation when the target and distractor were combined, while isolated fixation and optomotor responses were largely preserved. After 24 h of rest, attention-like behavior returned toward control levels. Matched mechanical stimulation with alternating rest periods did not produce the same impairment.

These controls support state-dependent disruption of selection beyond a general motor or visual failure. They do not identify a specific transmitter pathway or establish that flies have ADHD. The fly preparation tests visual competition and sleep state, whereas the mammalian tasks measure cue-guided choice, restraint or spatial working memory.

slides.title: Sleep-related rescue depends on fly genotype
body: Kirszenblat and colleagues compared wild-type flies with **dunce** and **rutabaga**, learning-related mutants with altered cAMP signaling. Dunce affects a cAMP-degrading phosphodiesterase; rutabaga affects a cAMP-producing adenylyl cyclase. Both mutants showed poorer visual selection and altered sleep relative to controls.

The sleep-promoting GABA-receptor agonist **THIP** was supplied at 0.1 mg/ml in food for 2 days and removed 1 h before testing. It increased sleep in both mutant backgrounds, but improved target selection in dunce rather than rutabaga. Wild-type improvement was not clearly established.

Genotype-dependent rescue supports separable relationships among sleep, molecular state and selection. It does not establish that the fly mutations reproduce mammalian prefrontal D1–HCN circuitry, or that manipulating cAMP has the same effect across species. A shared molecule does not guarantee an identical circuit, task computation or treatment response.

items.text: Accuracy, premature responses, delayed choice, working memory and locomotion measure different functions; an animal task phenotype does not establish a human ADHD diagnosis.
In the tested mouse task, LC projections to dorsomedial prefrontal cortex improved distractor resistance, while ventrolateral orbitofrontal targeting reduced premature responses.
Prefrontal-dependent reticular modulation changes geniculate inhibition and visual gain according to the selected sensory modality.
Adrenergic and D1 actions can sharpen prefrontal firing at suitable exposure; excessive D1 signaling can suppress delay activity through an HCN-sensitive mechanism.
NET contributes to frontal dopamine uptake; DAT deletion prolongs striatal signals, while SHR and Lphn3 models have distinct regional and drug-response profiles.
Sleep loss weakens fly selection under visual competition, and sleep-related rescue depends on genotype; shared behavioral measures or molecules do not establish identical circuits across species.
